sentences.text: The complainant told respondent no.1 that the items would be sold against receipt of the payment, to which respondent no.1 agreed.
Goods were, accordingly, delivered to respondent no. 1.
After delivery of goods, respondent no.1 issued cheque number 000067 dated 28.07.2016 for a sum of Rs. 20,400/- drawn on Bandhan Bank.
On 22.07.2016, complainant placed order for delivery of items for a sum of Rs. 1,48,171/- and gave a post-dated cheque payable after seven days.
Thereafter, respondent no.1 kept on placing orders on regular basis and goods were supplied to him in lieu of post-dated cheques.
On 26.07.2016, when the respondent no.1 placed an order for delivery of food items, complainant requested him to make the payment for the goods already delivery to him.
On this, respondent no.1 deposited Rs. 20,400/- in the account of the complainant.

Later, complainant supplied food items worth Rs. 51,298/- to respondent no.1 for which respondent no.1 issued a cheque of Rs. 51,000/-
and paid Rs. 298/- in cash.

Later, complainant came to know from the market that respondent no.1 did not pay for the goods purchased from the vendors.
Hence, he went to the house of the respondent no.1 where respondent no.2/sister of respondent no.1 and their mother met and gave three cheques to the complainant.
Thereafter, the complainant stopped delivering the goods to respondent no.1, as a large sum had become due.
He also came to know from one Ms. Shammi Kapoor that respondent no.1 had also taken goods from him, and that respondent no.1 owed Rs. 1.75 lac to him.
On enquiry, he also came to know that there were only few thousand rupees in the account of respondent no. 1 in Bandhan Bank and that several cheques issued by him in past had also been dishonoured.
On presentation, the cheques given by the respondent no.1 to the complainant also returned unpaid.

On 01.08.2016, when the employee of the complainant went to the house of respondent no.1 for demanding the payment against the dishonoured cheques, his employee met with one person who had come from Sonipat, Haryana and informed that he had also been cheated by respondent no.1 and that respondent no.1 owed Rs. 20 lac to him.
Thereafter, complainant made a complaint at police station but of no avail.

5. I have heard the arguments on behalf of the complainant.
Arguments were not addressed on behalf of the respondents despite several opportunities given to them.

6. In the instant case, petitioner examined himself as CW1 and Sh. Animesh, Branch Head of Bandhan Bank as CW2.
7.
In his testimony, CW1/petitioner has stated the facts alleged by him in his complaint whereas CW2 had produced the account statement of firm of the respondent no.1.

8. From the testimony of CW1, at this stage, it appears that he had delivered food items/goods to respondent no.1 for which respondent no.1 has allegedly issued post-dated cheques, which were dishonoured.

9. In his testimony, CW1 has also said that on enquiry the bank officials told him that the respondent did not maintain sufficient balance in his account and in past also several cheques issued by him had been dishonoured.

10. CW1 has also said that despite the assurance given by him Ravi Kumar Vs. Varun Monga & Anr.
Page no.4 of 7 after the intervention of the police, the respondent no.1 did not deposit the due amount in his bank account.

entities.text: Ravi Kumar Vs. Varun Monga & Anr
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 11. Apart from this, the complainant/CW1 has also said in his testimony that when he visited the place of business of the respondent no.1, after knowing that he had not paid the amount for the goods purchased from the other vendors in the market, he found that the premises was locked and the landlord informed him that the respondent had left the premises long ago.
The landlord also informed him that many persons and the police had also visited the premises and had enquired about the respondent.

12. Aforesaid fact shows that the respondent no.1 had disclosed to the complainant about his place of business, a premises which had been left by him long ago, which in turn shows that his intention was not honest since beginning.

13. Furthermore, respondent no.1 obtained goods from the complainant on the basis of the post-dated cheques without keeping sufficient balance in his bank account to honour the cheques,
consequently, on the presentation, the said cheques were dishonoured.

14. In Smt. Nagawwa vs. Veeranna Shivallngappa Konjalgi, AIR 1976 (SC) 1947, Hon'ble Apex Court held that an order of the Magistrate issuing process against the accused can be quashed or set aside only in following cases:
(A) Where the allegations made in the complaint, or the Ravi Kumar Vs. Varun Monga & Anr. Page no.5 of 7 statements of the witnesses recorded in support of the Sh. Ravi Kumar vs Sh. Varun Monga on 18 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/99397138/
3 same taken at their face value make out absolutely no case against the accused or the complaint does not disclose the essential ingredients of an offence which is alleged against the accused; (B) Where the allegations made in the complaint are patently absurd and inherently improbable so that no prudent person can ever reach a conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused;
(C) Where the discretion exercised by the Magistrate in issuing process is capricious and arbitrary having been based either on no evidence or on materials which are wholly irrelevant or inadmissible; and (D) Where the complaint suffers from fundamental legal defects, such as, want of sanction, or absence of a complaint by legally competent authority and the like.
15.

16. In the instant case, if the allegations made in the complaint and the statements of the witnesses are taken at their face value then it is found that there are material on record to show that the respondent no.2 had dishonest intention, since beginning, to cheat the complainant and therefore,

sentences.text: 17. Accordingly, there exists a prima facie case for summoning the respondent no.1/Sh. Varun Monga for commission of the cheating and dishonestly inducing the complainant for delivery of property, punishable under section 420 of IPC.
18. Having discussed as above, the revision is allowed, and the matter is remanded back to Ld. trial court to proceed with the matter in accordance with law.
19. Nothing said herein above, shall, however, be construed as any expression of opinion on the merits of the case.
